This paper identifies the covariance restriction required for a single latent correlation to summarize the relations between two clusters. The alignment ratios computed from the manifest covariances must be invariant with a common value of $\varphi^2$. Misassignment and misalignment both break this invariance, and when the invariance fails then no single population latent correlation exists for the cluster pair. Because the alignment ratios are computed directly from the manifest covariance matrix, they provide a descriptive diagnostic that may be reported alongside any fitted latent correlation without additional modeling.

## Alternatives to ICM-CFA

We have focused on ICM-CFA because it is perhaps the most popular model for assessing latent correlations.  Yet, there are several alternatives to ICM-CFA.  One is to retain a cluster structure but relax the constraint that tasks load on one and only one factor.  The resulting model is often called the exploratory structural equation model [ESEM, @Asparouhov.Muthen.2009; @Marsh.etal.2014; @Morin.etal.2016]. Allowing cross-cluster loadings reduces the need for the model to absorb cross-cluster covariance into the latent correlation.  As a result, ESEM models attenuate the inflation mechanisms described here, a fact that is emphasized in the ESEM literature. ESEM trades this benefit, however, for additional flexibility and ambiguity. Factor definitions depend on rotation and target specifications, and the resulting factor correlations may be sensitive to these choices. This flexibility can also weaken the simple cluster-based interpretation that motivates ICM-CFA in cognitive batteries, where factors are intended to map cleanly onto named constructs. For this reason, ESEM has been less widely adopted in cognitive-battery applications, despite its appeal as a remedy for cluster misassignment.  Moreover, permitting cross-loadings directly addresses misassignment-type misspecification, but it does not guarantee alignment of within-cluster and between-cluster submatrices.

Another alternative is the bifactor model, in which tasks load on both a general factor and a cluster-specific factor [@Holzinger.Swineford.1937; @Reise.2012]. Bifactor models can accommodate misalignment because the relative sizes of these loadings need not be the same across tasks. When proportionality holds, the relation between two clusters can be reduced to a single latent correlation through Equation \eqref{bifaclatcor}. With more than two clusters, extending this reduction requires rank-one structure among the latent correlations and leads to a hierarchical CFA representation [@Schmid.Leiman.1957; @Yung.etal.1999; @Brunner.etal.2012]. Proportionality, however, is not required for a bifactor model to be interpretable. Its general and cluster-specific factors can be meaningful without it [@Reise.2012; @Eid.etal.2017], and omega coefficients summarize how observed-score variance is distributed among them [@Rodriguez.etal.2016]. These interpretations do not require the covariance relations between clusters to reduce to a single latent correlation. They do, however, depend on whether the factors are appropriately defined by the underlying random experiment; when these requirements are not met, bifactor models may yield anomalous results and do not constitute a valid alternative to ICM-CFA [@Eid.etal.2017].

## Future Directions

Two future directions follow. First, it would be useful to develop formal methods for testing alignment-ratio invariance under sampling variability. One approach is to build test statistics in the spirit of vanishing tetrads and related constraint tests in factor analysis and SEM [@Wishart.1928; @Bollen.Ting.1993; @Drton.etal.2007], complemented perhaps by bootstrap procedures that assess the stability of invariance across resamples. Second, the alignment-ratio framework suggests a constructive route to cluster discovery. One could search for cluster partitions that yield approximately invariant alignment ratios, so that the resulting oblique factor structure admits a sound latent correlation. This could be implemented with combinatorial optimization. For example, one could minimize a dispersion measure of the alignment ratios (or a direct invariance criterion) over candidate partitions.
